title: Your payslip, line by line
description: A payslip looks crowded, but it tells one story: what you earned, what was taken off, and what you actually received.

body.heading: Start with the big number
paragraphs: The largest figure on a payslip is usually your gross pay: everything you earned before anything was taken away. If you are paid by the hour, it should match your hours multiplied by your hourly rate, with overtime shown separately.
It is worth a thirty-second check each payday. Mistakes happen, and they are far easier to fix in the week they occur than months later.

body.heading: The deductions in the middle
paragraphs: Between gross pay and the amount that lands in your account sits a list of deductions. Common ones include income tax, contributions toward pensions or social insurance, and sometimes student loan repayments or union fees.
These are not your employer keeping your money. They are amounts your employer is required to send onward on your behalf, and the payslip is your receipt proving it happened.

body.heading: The number to budget with
paragraphs: The final figure — net pay, or take-home pay — is what actually arrives in your account. It is the only honest number to build a budget on, because it is the money you can genuinely use.
Keep your payslips somewhere safe. Landlords, lenders, and tax offices may ask for them, and a tidy set of payslips is proof of income you will be glad to have.

takeaway: Budget from your net pay, check the gross against your hours, and keep payslips as proof of what you earned.
